newsitem.title: CHINA: China approves table grape imports from U.S..
newsitem.headline: China approves table grape imports from U.S..

text.p: China has given the go-ahead for imports of table grapes from the United States in another step towards resolving agricultural trade barriers between the two countries, U.S. agriculture officials said on Tuesday.

China's Administration of Animal and Plant Quarantine had informed U.S. agriculture officials that table grapes from four Californian counties could be exported to China from July 30, Ray Miyamoto, area director of the U.S. Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS), told Reuters.

The breakthrough was the result of a protocol negotiated in April, signed in May and followed up by an inspection tour of the Californian growing areas in June by Chinese quarantine officials, Miyamoto said.
The counties were Kern, Tulare, Fresno and Madera, he said.

China levies an 80 percent import tax on table grapes, but this was cut to 55 percent because Washington extends most-favoured nation trading status to Beijing, U.S. sources said. A value-added tax of 13 percent also applied, they said.
The Chinese go-ahead signalled an acceptance by the Chinese that U.S. quarantine techniques were adequate for ensuring a safe export product, another U.S. official said.
California declared itself free of the Mediterranean fruit fly on June 14, 1996, but Chinese quarantine had not officially accepted it was a safe area, he said on condition of anonymity.

"Quarantine laws had limited us before California eradicated the Med fly, but now they (the Chinese) are recognising that we can export fruit even from areas that do have pests, but which are controlled by measures that ensure we get a safe product to them," the official said.
Fruit has long been a sore point between Washington and Beijing, and the subject of exhaustive negotiations on phytosanitary, or plant health, issues.
Conditions for exports to China of U.S. citrus fruit are yet to be worked out as the areas in question, most notably Florida, still had pest problems, another official said.
A number of protocols have been signed in recent years, most pertaining to Beijing's application to join the international free trade club, the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
In June, the first official shipment of U.S. cherries arrived in China -- subject to 48 percent import duty plus a value-added tax -- under agreements reached in a 1995 protocol.
And last month two containers of lychees, the first Chinese fruit ever to be exported to the United States, left southern China for California.
U.S. officials said on Monday that recent negotiating offers China had made in its efforts to join the WTO were inadequate, and a broad range of concerns still needed to be addressed.

Those issues ranged from market access to transparency in government procurement and business transactions, to reduction of tariffs and the elimination of non-tariff trade barriers to trade, to subsidies, the official, said.
Among the non-tariff trade barriers Washington has long railed against is Beijing's ban on wheat imports from the Pacific northwest region of the United States.
Beijing says a fungus it carries called TCK smut could harm its own wheat crop, though Washington insists it is harmless.
A U.S. source said on Tuesday the wheat question was at a stalemate and was now being dealt with as a trade issue by the U.S. Foreign Agriculture Service.
